The ALTOS Framework, Principle 3: Every Document Has an Owner

By Ambrosio “Butch” U. Mahinay

A receipt that belongs to everyone belongs to no one. Every form in custody and every peso in hand needs a named, bonded officer who answers for it.

Imagine a booklet of official receipts lying on a desk that three clerks share. One page is missing. Who explains it? If the honest answer is “we are not sure,” the office has a problem, and it is not a problem about honesty. It is a problem about ownership.

Accountability needs a name. Every form in custody and every peso in hand should have one person who answers for it, and that person should be bonded.

Why a Name Matters: The Principal and the Agent

Economists have a useful way of describing this. Principal–agent theory, developed by Michael Jensen, William Meckling and others, looks at any relationship in which one party, the principal, relies on another, the agent, who knows more and whose interests may differ. The usual remedies are contracts, monitoring and incentives that narrow the gap in information.

Local government is a long chain of such relationships. Citizens elect the governor or mayor and the Sanggunian. These officials rely on the treasurer. The treasurer relies on the collecting officers. At every link, the person doing the work knows more than the person who depends on it. The theory does not assume anyone is dishonest. It only assumes that information is uneven.

Accountable forms, fidelity bonds, reports with deadlines and audit trails are all tools for closing that gap. And none of them works unless each one is tied to a specific person. This is the economic logic behind what I call 360° accountability: a named officer answerable at every point of the circle.

One Officer, One Superior

Henri Fayol, writing in 1916, listed unity of command among his principles of management: each person should take orders from one superior. In a treasury this means each collecting officer answers to one liquidating officer, who answers to the treasurer. Max Weber would recognize the rest. A collector is assigned to a particular market or barangay, which is a fixed jurisdiction, and the hierarchy runs upward from collector to liquidating officer to treasurer.

When two people share one booklet, or a collector reports to whoever happens to be around, the chain breaks, and with it the ability to say who is responsible.

Luther Gulick's list of an executive's duties points the same way. In a treasury, Staffing means designating bonded collecting, liquidating and disbursing officers, and Directing means assigning each one a collection area and putting it in an office order. Ownership starts with a written assignment.

Who Holds What

An accountable officer is any official or employee whose duties require custody of government funds, property or accountable forms. In a local treasury the main roles are:

Collecting officer. Holds official receipts and the cash collected, and answers for every receipt in custody, used or unused, and every peso until it is deposited or remitted.

Liquidating officer. Receives the collectors' remittances and reports, checks each collector's RCD, consolidates collections, and prepares the monthly CRAAF.

Disbursing officer. Holds cash advances for payroll or petty expenses and answers for liquidating each one within the required period.

Treasurer. Has overall custody of funds, checks and forms, and answers for the whole treasury, including the acts of subordinates where supervision failed.

That last line deserves attention. The treasurer's accountability is not only for what the treasurer personally touches. It extends to what the treasurer should have been watching.

What the Government Auditing Code Says

Presidential Decree 1445 puts this into law. Every officer whose duties involve the possession or custody of government funds or property is accountable for them and liable for their safekeeping. The head of the agency carries primary responsibility for all funds and property under it, and those who handle them are directly accountable to the head. And under Section 101, every accountable officer must be properly bonded.

The Fidelity Bond

A fidelity bond stands behind the officer: if public money in that officer's care is lost through the officer's fault, the government has a way to be made whole. Both Section 101 of PD 1445 and Section 305 of the Local Government Code require it. The Bureau of the Treasury administers the bonding system under its Revised Omnibus Regulations, Treasury Circular No. 02-2009, as later amended.

Two details are easy to forget. First, the amount of the bond should follow the size of the accountability. A collector who now handles far more cash than when the bond was first set may be bonded for far too little without anyone noticing. Second, bonds expire. An officer whose bond lapsed last month is, on paper, holding public money with no guarantee behind it.

Distance Calls for Stronger Ownership

Money is collected at the treasury windows, but also at markets and terminals, on barangay collection days, and through banks. Every one of these points needs a named collecting officer with forms in custody. The farther a collection point is from the office, the stronger the controls must be, because supervision there is weaker. Ownership is the control that travels with the collector.

Accountability in Four Directions

Public administration usually describes accountability in three directions: upward to superiors and oversight bodies, downward to citizens, and sideways to peer offices and auditors. ALTOS adds a fourth direction: across time. A record must be just as trustworthy five years from now, under a different treasurer, as it is today. That is only possible if the record still says, years later, exactly who was responsible.

Where ALTOS Helps

In ALTOS, every series of receipts and every check booklet is assigned to a named officer, and each user has one role that shows only the pages that role needs. An officer cannot act for another officer. When the System Administrator opens another user's page to help, every action there is recorded as done by the administrator acting for that user, so the name on the record is always the true one.

The system also keeps each officer's bond amount and expiry date. By default it warns 60 days before a bond lapses. It compares each bond with the cash the officer actually handled and flags any bond that is missing, expired or too low. A rule that used to live in a filing cabinet has become a daily reminder on the screen.

The Question to Ask

Who is answerable, and are they bonded? Put more sharply: is every accountable officer bonded today, for the right amount? The evidence is a current bond for every accountable officer, matched to what each one actually handles.

Owners give documents their force. But an owner with no due date can always say “I will get to it later,” and later can stretch for months. The fourth principle closes that gap: every owner has a deadline.

When did your office last check every accountable officer's bond against what they actually handle? I'd be glad to hear what you found. Email me.
